Why are these salaries dealt with in the Estimates instead of by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to increase the salaries it is necessary to deal with them here. That is the reason why we retain some of our officials:	I think
they are all certainly not overpaid. I may ,say, following the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that I think we lost one of the best officials we had in Mr. Henry T. Ross. Mr. Ross was the Assistant Deputy Minister of the Department of Finance at a salary of $4,000. I think it was increased to $4,500. He came to me and told me of an offer he had received from outside. He was very reluctant to leave the service, but I felt I should not stand in his way, because I could not, without upsetting the entire Civil Service, pay him anything like the salary he was offered. The result was that a man worth $10,000 to the department was lost, and I have missed him almost every day since he left. He is now receiving a salary two or three times more than he received from the Dominion Government.

Let me add, to make myself clear, that I am not offering any

captious criticism. It does seem to me now, and it has seemed to me on other occasions, that in our Civil Service we are very much like the army. I do not want to detract in any way from the generals and the other high officials who are really responsible for the conduct of the army, but I have thought some times that the glory which goes to those in high command is a glory which very often has passed on to them from those in the ranks. I apply my comparison to the Civil Service in the same way, that we hear a great deal in this House from time to time about the excellence of men who are drawing $4,000, $5,000, $6,000, or $7,000 a year, and I think a great deal of their excellence is due perhaps to the fact that they have efficient civil servants under them who are drawing from $1,200 to $1,400 a year and finding it hard work to make a living. That is what I mean. I have not seen during this session or in any previous session that consideration given for those in the lower ranks of the Civil Service which in my estimation they should receive; and I have seen what seems to be a disposition in this session and in previous sessions to give consideration, more perhaps than is their due, to men who occupy high positions in the Government service and drawing $5,000, $6,000 or $7,000 a year. I hope I have made myself clear. That, at all events, is my view in regard to the matter. What is the use of your so-called experts from Chicago who have reclassified and undertaken to fix the salaries of the civil servants? It means, if the words of the Finance Minister mean anything, that their . classification and arrangement of salaries will apply to men in the lower walks of the Civil Service, but when it suits the minister of any department to tack on a thousand dollars to the salary of a deputy minister or of an assistant deputy minister, or of any person who is getting three or four times the salary that is drawn by another man who is doing efficient service, that may be dealt with here in this House. We must not undertake to deal with, nor would it be proper on the part of members to consider improving the salaries of civil servants getting $1,200, $1,400 or $1,500 a year. We must be limited, we must not have anything to say in regard to those men, their positions or their salaries; but if a man gets from $5,000 to $7,000 a year, then if the reclassification does not 'touch that man, there is a way to tack another thousand dollars onto his salary.

Estimates came down I looked through them to see if certain civil servants had got an increase; I found they were not dealt with. I understood a little over a year ago when the Civil Service Commission was appointed that the work would be left in their hands. But I would point out that now patronage is taken from the back benches and handed over to a few members of the Government so they can give what salaries they like. A year ago Parliament appointed a re-classification committee, and I think that every hon. member and every man and woman throughout Canada, in view of the prevailing unrest and discontent, believed the Government would be the first to set an example and would not do anything to augment that unrest and discontent. Now when the report of that classification committee comes down, what do we find? We find men's salaries being increased from $100 to $2,000 by this Government, while we have been paying $150 a day to the men who were making that report. The Government was well aware that that report was coming down at any time. First of all we were told it would be brought down in two or three weeks, then we were told it would be ready in April, and the next time we were told it would be placed before us in May. In the very face of that this Government added $500,$1,000, and in some cases $2,000 to the salaries of civil servants whom that committee rated lower than men who were getting $1,000 less. When I asked the question on the floor of this House, if it was the intention of the Government to accept that classification, to bring every man up to it, or down to it, I was told that was not the intention. Can we expect harmony and union in the country when the Government, during the present session, gives .to one man drawing $5,000 a year an additional $500, and nothing to another man who is drawing $4,000 a year, although the man drawing $4,000 a year is rated at $4,800 by the classification committtee, and the man drawing $5,000 a year is rated at $4,500? What will be the result? The man rated at $4,500 will continue to draw $5,000-$200 more than the man who is rated at $4,800 and drawing $4,000. There is not a Cabinet minister or an hon. member to-day if he knew he had the right to $200 or $300 a year more thah .another man, would be satisfied that the other man should continue to draw more. But that is what we are told in this House is to happen, and is it any wonder we have

discontent? I say we have the right to have those men reduced according to that classification when it is adopted, or, if they are below it we must raise them up to it.
I can give you one case where a civil servant drawing $4,500 a year had another $500 added to his salary during this present session, >and the classification reports him at $2,280.

speechtext:

Canadian Press Limited-towards expenses of a national news service, $50,000.
What are the ramifications of the Canadian press? How is it worked out? What is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The memorandum which I have is as follows:
The Canadian Press Limited is an incorporated news agency of which all publishers of daily newspapers in Canada are members and stockholders. It does not operate to make a profit; the expenses of operation are assessed against the individual newspapers according to an established basis. The Government grant is to be applied towards the expense of maintaining a day and night leased wire news service over the three great natural gaps, namely, between Ottawa and Winnipeg, Oalgary and Vancouver, and Montreal and Saint John. The bridging of these gaps will make it possible. for this association to operate a national news service from coast to coast.
The motive of the grant of $50,000 is to enable the better distribution of Canadian news throughout the entire Dominion.

Earlier in the session I moved the following resolution in connection with the press:
That in the opinion of this House, all newspapers, magazines, trade journals and other periodicals, publishing articles designed to mnu-ence public opinion shall be compelled from time to time to publish sworn statements setting forth the names of the owners, managers, editors, stockholders, bondholders and of any other person having an interest in such newspaper, magazine, trade journal or other periodical.
I do not object to the grant of $50,000 to the Canadian, press. I am an old journalist, and I believe in the press; I believe that it should be given all the facilities possible in order to enable it, by means of its editorial and news columns, to spread knowledge all over the country. But, for the reasons which I have already given, I think that the pres? of Canada should be subject to the. same rule-I should say, to the same law-that prevails in the United States. The subject was fully discussed in the House on two or three occasions, and the President of the Council promised me that sometime during the session 'he would announce the policy of the Government in connection with this matter. Perhaps my hon. friend will take advantage of this opportunity of informing the committee whether the Government intends to adopt the principle enunciated in this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
At the time I pointed
out to my hon. friend that the matter covered by his resolution was within the jurisdiction of the various provincial legislatures, and that any province which desired to have the information covered by his resolution furnished and made public, had full legislative power to do so. My hon. friend suggested that the Federal Government might take action along lines similar to that taken in the United States. I have had the law looked into, and when the Prime Minister returned I submitted the matter to him. Owing, however, to the desire to conclude this session at the earliest possible date-.and my hon. friend is aware of the amount of legislation already introduced-the Government decided not to introduce any legislation in connection with the matter at this session. It was not considered of such an urgent character as to necessitate its being introduced in the closing hours of the session.

Before this item passes,
I should like to register a most temperate but, I trust, most emphatic protest against this subsidy to the press. When this Government had no paper of its own, there

was perhaps more excuse, although I do not think, reason for this subsidy of a very substantial amount. But this Government has gone, with the aid of the President of the Council, into the newspaper business. We have the Official Canadian Record containing the information which the Government thinks it 'wise to distribute amongst the people, and I think that costs several tens of thousands dollars a year. The President of the Council will correct me if I am wrong. Why then should the Government be bonusing its competitors? If the Government is in the newspaper business why give the people's money to aid its competitors? That is the first point I want to make. A feeling exists in the country-and I think it is well founded- that the newspaper press, in receiving this money is, perhaps, somewhat influenced in favour of the donors. I do not wish to say that emphatically because I have not the proof, but the tendency is that, when you are in receipt of gifts from a person, you regard that person with, perhaps, a more benevolent eye than you otherwise would. Some newspapers in this country make money; other papers make no money, but. those who make money are certainly not in need of governmental assistance for the purpose of getting news, and it is a question whether those who do not make money can be saved from bad financial condition by whatever assistance this grant is to them. I have an abhorrence of any governmental influence, directly or indirectly, upon the press. It is the most unwholesome condition that can possibly exist in this country. I know that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) sometimes passes restless and worried hours when he considers the financial condition of the country, because I believe he is a patriotic citizen who has some appreciation, though with all humility and courtesy, 1 think, inadequate consideration of the very serious condition in which our finances are. What could he do better than either to cut out this allowance of $50,000 very substantially or to cut it out altogether? I point that way of economy. When we speak of economy on this side of the House, we are often told that we make vain and general observations, and we should come down to specific instances. I do not wish to detain the committee, as we are trying to finish the work of the session, but I would ask the Minister of Finance to consider very carefully whether he would not be able to save some of the people's money in cutting down this -grant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It does not appear to me that this grant of $50,000 to the Canadian Press, Limited, will have any influence upon the newspapers of this country.
I doubt very much if the great majority of them have it in their mind that the grant is made. The purpose of the grant was in the national interest. This country is peculiar geographically; we have a gap of one thousand miles between East and West; we have another gap between the prairies and the Pacific coast, and so between Montreal and the Maritime Provinces.
Mr. MoMASTER: The minister forgets Quebec, Sherbrooke, and other important places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of this is to enable the different portions of this country to receive more news of other parts than they otherwise would. If we cut out this	grant, my belief	is that	theWestern press will not receive from the East the news service that it does to-day. Hon. gentlemen may say: Well, let them receive an inferior service. My view is that, in a country of the size of Canada, with our sparse population, a grant of this kind for the purpose we have in view	can	serve a good nationalpurpose.	It	is not a	large	sumof money, and what appealed to the Government and to .myself, because I believe I was responsible for the introduction of the item originally-was the improvement of the service between East and West in this country, so that the people living in the West would get to know more about what was going on in the East, and vice versa. In that way	this	small grant	would	tend
towards bringing about a better understanding and closer harmony between all parts of the country.

It is easy to defend the grant which was made some years ago by my hon. friend's predecessor (Mr. Fielding) to the cable news service from England. I remember that that hon. gentleman, when he was Minister of Finance, granted a subsidy of, I think, $15,000 a year for a cable news service from London to 'Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the next item.

But this grant of $50,000 for the Canadian press in Canada I do not feel inclined to defend so easily. The amount, however, is there, and I think under those circumstances the Government should accept the principle of my resolution. I must

say to the President of the Council that this resolution has been adopted at all conventions held in the western provinces during the last few years, and it is an exact copy of those resolutions which is to-day on the Order Paper. My hon, friend (Mr. Rowell) says that there is a question of provincial rights in connection with this resolution. He is able to obviate the difficulty if such is the difficulty. By the Post Office Act the department can make their own regulations. As I have already stated, for the important privilege enjoyed by the press in transmission through the mails of newspapers at a very cheap rate, practically nothing, the Government in return should ask the newspapers to give the public the moral guarantee which we find embodied in the Congressional law. I give notice to my hon. friend that if the Government does not act this year, I intend at the next session to move again this resolution, and my hon. friend should not "wait until the dying hours of the session to announce that the Government has had no time to consider this matter.

I heartily concur in the view of the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) as regards the object of the resolution that he has on the Order Paper. I believe that a newspaper ought to be obliged to publish the names of its proprietors. Newspapers representthemselves as being published in the interest of the public, and I believe the public have an absolute right to know the names of the proprietors, to know absolutely what is behind the print.
Had the hon. gentleman had the opportunity of moving his resolution in the ordinary way I should have taken great pleasure in supporting it. Permit me to add a word to what the Minister of Finance said with regard to the main reason why this subsidy was granted. For a great many years the news that was furnished to the newspapers in the Canadian Northwest filtered through American channels from St. Paul and Minneapolis and was distributed in Winnipeg to the Western papers. It cost very much less to bring the news from St. Paul and Minneapolis, but the news being from American sources was coloured. From time to time the newspaper associations discussed the situation and eventually it came to the ear of the Government that the matter should be remedied. It was absolutely impossible for the newspapers in the West to carry a leased wire around the north shore of Lake Superior to distribute
[Mr. L.emienx.11
the news collected from purely Canadian sources; so a subsidy was proposed, and coupled with it was the request that the gap be bridged to the Maritime Provinces. I agree with the minister that not all the newspapers know about this subsidy. It is not given to influence any newspaper. All the papers profit equally by it. If the money were distributed among the different papers it would be a very small amount. I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) would insinuate that any paper would allow its policy to be influenced by the fact that it might profit in some cases by the subsidy.

The Minister of Finance said a few moments ago that the Canadian Press Association was a joint stock corporation operating without profit. How are the shares held? Are they paid for in any way, who are the officials of the company, what salaries are they paid, and how is the grant distributed?

Perhaps I can answer that question. The officers of the Canadian Press receive no pay whatever. They are confined to president, vice-president, secretary-treasurer, and directors. All the daily papers of the Dominion are members of the association. They are all shareholders, but are not all directors. The shares are divided into one hundred dollars each, I believe, and each newspaper throughout the Dominion gets one share. I am not sure whether they pay for it, but probably they do.
Who are the members of the board?

There is one in Vancouver, one in Victoria, one in Calgary, two in Winnipeg, two or three in Toronto, two or three in Montreal, one in Halifax, one in Moncton, one in Hamilton, and one in London, I believe.
Are both parties represented?

Certainly. Politics does not enter into the constitution of the association in any way whatsoever. There are no profits made, and no dividends declared. In fact, very frequently there are assessments because of the increased cost of collecting news. Nobody makes a farthing out of it. Notwithstanding the subsidy, I regret to say that you could count on the fingers of one hand, certainly on the fingers of two, the newspapers that have been able to make ends meet during the last four or five years.
What is the method of distributing the money, where does it go tor

The money is paid into the Canadian Press Association, whose head office is in Toronto. It is used for the purpose of paying for the leased wire from Vancouver to the Atlantic coast. That costs a very large sum of money. I fancy the subsidy would be all absorbed by that charge.	N
Is this the association that maiiaged the advertising campaign for the Union Party in 1917?
It has nothing whatever to do with managing any election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been
handed a note from the Press Gallery in which it is stated that the London Advertiser, Le Soleil, Le Canada, and all other Liberal papers in the Dominion share in the Canadian, press service. It has not been drawn to my attention that these papers were very active in supporting the Union Government at the last election.

That scarcely answers my question. We are all well aware of the stand the London Advertiser took in the 1917 election. My hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) said that one of the reasons for this subsidy was that the papers of the Canadian Northwest were receiving coloured news from American sources. Unfortunately, I am afraid there is a strong suspicion -I do not know how well founded it is- that the information supplied through the Canadian Press Association is also coloured, that it is not as fair to both parties as it might be. I am afraid that the papers who receive this subsidy are unconsciously influenced by it.

The affairs of the
association are governed entirely by the directors, who are selected from papers utterly regardless of their political predilections. I am one of the directors and I know that it has rarely happened, not more than twice I believe, that a complaint has been made that the reports were not absolutely fair and non-partisan. No official of the association is ever asked a question as to his politics. The directors endeavour to deal with absolute fairness and justice in the collection and distribution of news, and the news is sent out to papers regard-lesss of their politics. I think my hon. friend would be perfectly satisfied if he Tead the reports that are sent out. .

I am not familiar with the details of the distribution of this
money, but so far as the principle of the grant is concerned, while the Minister of Finance has taken the responsibility for it,
I must be willing to associate myself in some degree with that responsibility because it is the carrying out of a policy which was begun by the Government of which I was a member, and which was partially successful, as has been mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). I formed a very strong opinion, and my colleagues agreed with me, that it was highly desirable that provision should be made for the better dissemination of news as between Canada and Great Britain, and also between eastern and western Canada. With regard to the cable service, while it was not always free from criticism, it is generally admitted that we did get a direct cable service from the Old Country which made us independent of the connection with the United States, and while sometimes it did not give us all that we desired, it was very helpful and in the right direction. With regard to the home service the Government are carrying out a policy which I confess I attempted to carry out with only very limited success. I formed the impression and my colleagues agree with me that it was highly important that there should be better communication between eastern and western Canada. We were bringing into Canada hundreds of thousands of immigrants who landed at Montreal or Quebec, and then went across to western Canada. They knew absolutely nothing of eastern Canada, which formed a part of the Dominion. They were going out there unacquainted with the affairs of our country. The information that was given to them was limited at the best, and what did go to them came largely through communication with the United States.	t
At a very early stage in the experience of our Government, I confess now, we took up this very question and I personally visited some of the journalists in western Canada and endeavoured to get just such an organization as the hon. gentleman now has, At that time I did not succeed because the newspapers were not numerous enough and were not able to bear the burden and although I was prepared to recommend to my colleagues the granting of a subsidy I was not assured of a sufficient response from the press to justify me in carrying the matter any further. The object was to let the eastern people of Canada know something about the people of that western country and to let the western people get fuller information about eastern Canada

than they had been getting. I think the object is a good one and I see no reason why it should not be supported.

I am afraid that when the party in power is distributing this money, there is a possibility, if not a probability, of influencing the press. I might give the Finance Minister just one specific instance of the news being coloured by the press in the last election. Sir Allen Ayles-worth is one of the best known publicists in Canada. During the last election he delivered a most important speech in Toronto. No adequate report of that speech appeared, in so far as I know, in any paper in Canada east of Toronto.
Nor west.

Nor west of Toronto either. Is it not most essential that the views, whether they be the views of the minority or the majority, of public men, should be distributed without any favour? It does seem to me that the Government would have a little advantage by distributing the news which is most important for the Government, In a -subsidized distribution the tendency will be to distribute the news which the Government in office thinks is of interest to the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The best judges of the news value of -any speech are the press. I have frequently been in the position of making what I regarded as a very able speech, and, upon looking for the report next morning in the press I found about half a "stick." I have come to the conclusion after such experience as I have had that probably the newspapers themselves have a much better sense of values than the makers of speeches. While I am the last person to in -any way disparage the standing of Sir Allen Aylesworth, whom I know very well personally, at the same time I am of the view that the newspapers which report speeches fairly correctly appraise their news value.
I	think my hon. friend will find
that the press in many cases have paid comparatively little attention to the speeches which we on this side might regard as of a particularly destructive, or constructive, character. Personally I think that a public man is fortunate to be reported at all. All of us feel frequently that the reports of our speeches are more or less garbled but as I become older in. public life I am not disconsolate at seeing even a garbled report given of my speech, and I make no complaint at all.

I had nothing whatever to do with the arrangements for this Canadian Press but I did have something to do with the organization of the cable service. As soon as that service was established one of the main conditions that we insisted upon was that the Government should have" nothing to do with it at all, and that it should be administered by an association of newspapermen who would manage it for themselves. We stipulated that the Government should have nothing to do with it except to provide the money and as a result the management of it in London was placed in the hands of the Toronto Telegram.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Take this particular item which has been voted for the last three years-/I never knew when it was paid to the Canadian Press Limited. It is paid by cheque by some officer of the department.
What we are afraid of Is not the possibility of the press coming to the Government but of some members of the Government going to the press. _

The Government, before they dealt with the press at all, insisted that there should be a national organization built up by the Canadian press to cover the entire country. They insisted upon that before they would agree to grant the subsidy. That has been done. The Government has nothing to do with the distribution of that grant. It is paid out as the Finance Minister says. With the large foreign population in the Northwest it was felt that they should have the right kind of literature distributed to them through the press.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
While this item is before the- committee, I wish to refer to a question that has been previously raised in the House, and which has been frequently discussed in the press for the purpose of put-

ting on record for the information of the members of the House certain facts in relation to the numbers of Orders in Council "'which have been passed in recent years and particularly under the War Measures Act.
Various statements have appeared in the press as to the ever-increasing number of Orders in Council which were being passed by the Government particularly under Union government. The most striking statement appeared in Le Devoir of 7th December last, and for the information of the members I shall read the paragraph that appeared in that paper:
From the first of July, 1867, to the 20th April, 1918,
the different governments which have succeeded one another at Ottawa have adopted in all 919 Orders in Council. Guided by Mr. Kowell, the Unionist Minister, in six months, from the 20th April to the 23rd October, 1918, the Government has adopted and sighed 1,667 Orders in all, of which many hundreds were passed even while Parliament was in session, and among them those which radically suppressed the liberty of the press and of public opinion, and annulled at one stroke, at a secret meeting of the Cabinet, the exemption of thousands and thousands of young men from twenty to twenty-three years of age who had been liberated for proper motives by competent tribunals, and sent them to service in the army.
I should like to draw the attention of the. committee to the comparative statement contained in that paragraph, namely, that in fifty-one years, or more, prior to the date when I had the honour to become President of the Privy [Council, some 919 Orders in Council were passed and that in six months, while I was President of the Privy Council, 1,667 had been passed. For the information of the members of the committee, I might say that while I have not the exact record, the total number of Orders in [Council passed from the 1st of July, 1867, to the 31st December, 1917, was approximately-not 919, but 145,000. That is a fine illustration of exaggeration with a view of making a point against the Government.
May I interrupt a moment to ask the Chairman to tell me what item we haye under consideration which brings forth this interesting information?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Privy Council Estimates, tTetails of which are to be found at page 12 of the Estimates. Then, with reference to the Orders in Council passed in recent years, I have the figures from 1910-
Will the minister pardon me just a moment? May I ask whether he is dealing with the salaries of officials?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am dealing with the general question of civil government and making a statement with respect to the work of the Privy Council.
May I ask the Chairman to rule whether the minister is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it that the statement is being made with the unanimous consent of the Committee, as is the custom upon the opening up of the Estimates of a particular department. However, if the hon. member insists upon his point I must rule that the statement is not in order upon the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It has one interesting effect: It brings all the sins of the Orders in Council home to the Privy 'Council office.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are but the medium through which the orders pass, hut, of course, we have the record of them. If the hon. gentleman objects, I cannot give the further information which is 'available.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not objecting.
Is it not part of the duties of the officials whose salaries we are being asked to vote, to write out these Orders in Council? Have these officials any work in connection with Orders in Council?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already ruled that the statement would be in order with the unanimous consent of the Committee, and that it is a statement such as is given by all ministers in presenting tlheir Estimates.

If the paternity of these Orders in 'Council rests on the conscience of the President of the Privy Council and he wishes to free his conscience by making this statement, I withdraw my objection in order to give him a free field.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

Mines and Geological Survey Department- For experimental work relating to briquetting ot lignite coal (Revote), $160,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
A number of. 'members have spoken to me about this particular item, Mr. Chairman, and I would like very briefly to state the position of this work. As the result of a recommendation by the Research Council, approved by the Reconstruction Committee, it was decided to authorize the Minister of Mines to enter into agreements with the Provincial Governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, by which each Provincial Government would grant $100,000 and this Government $200,000 for the purpose of investigating the lignite deposits of Saskatchewan and putting up a plant to briquette the lignite and put it on the market as a commercial fuel, in view of the scarcity of coal and the enormous cost of the anthracite coming into that market. Agreements were entered into with the two provinces, and subsequently a Lignite Utilization Board was appointed, consisting of Mr. R. A. Ross, consulting engineer, of Montreal, who is a member of the Research Council; Mr. Sheppart, of Moosejaw, and Mr. Leamy, an engineer of the city of Winnipeg. They discussed the whole situation and surveyed all the work that had been done in connection with briquetting. They appointed a staff of two engineers-one of whom was placed at their disposal from our own department, Mr. San-field. an engineering chemist-who inspected ail the different briqueMmg plants in the United States. It was thought that perhaps a lot of valuable information might be secured to guide us in Saskatchewan. However, it appears that nothing had been done

in the United States', except in respect to bituminous coal, and there was practically little to help us in reference to the immediate question we had under consideration. When this information had been gathered these two gentlemen made a trip to the Western part of Canada, samples were taken of the lignite coal in the Estevan district, and every kind of information contributory to the question was gathered there and studied to see if the briquetting process was a commercial possibility. Subsequently it appeared from their investigation that the whole matter depended on the carbonization7 of lignite. Lignite, as honourable members know, occurs in enormous deposits in Saskatchewan, and if it could be placed on the market in a suitable form it would be of great help in solving the fuel question. But lignite contains a heavy percentage of moisture, it rapidly disintegrates, and is then not particularly useful from the commercial point of view. The question, therefore, was to see if a process could be divised by which the calorific value of lignite, which is only half that of anthracite, could be put in such a form that the excess water could be driven out and the whole product, by a process of briquetting, made to approach to something like the value of anthracite pound for pound. A good deal of experimental work has been done. It was found, however, that we could not this year go on with the erection of the necessary briquetting plant as contemplated and hoped for. We determined, and I think wisely, not to incur that expense until we had thoroughly demonstrated the successful operation of the carbonizing process. We could drive out the excess moisture by the ordinary heating process or by air, but even then the product would rapidly absorb moisture again. The only practical way was by means of carbonization, which consists of heating the lignite to a high temperature in the absence of air, which would drive off not only the moisture but the various gases, and leave a product very much smaller in bulk and very much higher in calorific value. We have had a great deal of difficulty devising a carbonizing plant by which	this could	be satisfactorily
demonstrated, but finally a plant was designed and has lately been installed in the Mines Department, and that part of the experimental work is being carried on at the	present moment.
A good deal of experimental work is being carried on in connection with the binders for the making of briquettes, and progress
is being made. So far as standard machinery can be used in the briquetting and in other necessary processes, we are computing, subject to the soundness of carbonization experiments, what it would cost commercially in the way of machinery and buildings to establish a plant for the production of these lignite briquettes. If the carbonizer which is now being installed works as we have every reason to believe it will work and if the development of the binder experiment is satisfactory-and we have reason to believe that it is-I think we shall be in a position, in about two months, to select a place where the plant may be put up, to commence construction, and to get the thing under way. In that case we would probably be able to deliver fuel by 1920 and 1921. To members of the West who may think that there has been some delay in this matter I may point out that we would not have been justified in expending this $400,000 in the hasty erection of a large plant to briquette lignite on a commercial scale unless we had first made absolutely sure of our ground. That points to the reason why these experiments have been carried on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Experiments in briquetting of bituminous coal have been satisfactorily carried on in Nova Scotia, though not to a very great extent. Have the experiments to which my hon. friend refers been able to show whether a ton of briquette lignite can be sold in the market as at a price which compares favourably with that of, say, bituminous coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Well, one cannot be
positive in answering that question, but there is every reason to believe that the production of this article will be commercially successful. Of course, the lignite question is a little different from that of bituminous coal. One of the sources of profit in the carbonization of bituminous coal is in the by-products which are very valuable, whereas the by-products of lignite coal are comparatively small so far as coal value goes. But if we can once get the carbonizing experiment to a proper stage of development, I believe that this business can be made absolutely a commercial success.
Mines Branch, $309,OW).

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This includes an amount for the carrying on of experimental work in connection with peat. Some time ago there was a very interesting discussion in this House and a very interesting controversy in the country on the vexed ques-

tion whether peat could be made a commercial fuel. Something like 140,000,000 tons of peat are known to be available in Canada; probably $30,000,000 have been spent during the last thirty or forty years in this country on experiments with peat, most of them having been doomed to failure for one reason or another. The result of all our investigations was to show that the whole question was one of the cheap handling of the raw material. It is absolutely necessary to the commercial success of the handling of peat that some form of machinery be devised to handle the raw material in such a cheap and economic way that when put on the market it will compete with the ordinary prices of anthracite or bituminous coal. We went into the matter thoroughly about a year ago and we found that as there are many peat bogs in Ontario, the Government of that province was also interested in the question. We finally made an arrangement with the 5 p.m. Ontario Government under which a certain sum of money was set aside and a joint committee was appointed to study the whole question and to conduct experiments. Two types of machinery were adopted, one designed by an expert in this business, Mr. E. V. Moore, and another an adaptation of the old Anrep plant. Mr. Anrep, senior, used to be the most noted expert in this line in Sweden. Part of his machines were used in the Alfred bogs in Ontario some years ago. As a result of the operations there a certain amount of success was achieved, but a good deal of doubt was cast upon the commercial value of the product. Last year, therefore, a committee was appointed consisting of Mr. P. A. Ross, of the Research Council, Montreal; Mr. Cole, of the Ontario Government; Mr. Haanel, of the Mines Department, and Mr. Harris. They worked on the various designs for peat machinery, and one of the machines was nearly ready by December but was held up owing to various causes: failure of-the manufacturers to deliver, the epidemic of influenza and causes arising out of the war; so that we were not able to get any work done. But we have made arrangements to operate on the Alfred bog, which is' about forty miles from Ottawa, and one of. the machines has commenced to manufacture peat there on a commercial scale at the rate of about sixty or seventy tons a day. The other machine should be ready to start next week.
What would be the cost of production per ton?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is impossible to say that. Experiments which were conducted some years ago in the Alfred bog showed that, with the price of labour as it was then, the product could almost compete with the price of anthracite prevailing at that time. But having regard to the increased cost of labour and to other conditions, I should not like to venture an assertion as to the cost at the present time. The question really is whether it is & practical proposition to develop Canada's enormous peat resources, or whether we should abandon the idea altogether. I myself am hopeful that as a result of the work which is being done this year we shall be able to show that by employing proper engineer-d&vices and using proper machinery, it will be possible to manufacture air-dried peat of this kind on such a cost basis as will make it a very useful 'adjunct to our future fuel supply. That of course is a thing which one would not like to pronounce upon.
Mr. (McKENZIE: Does the minister think that we have real peat in this country? Did he ever have it compared with Scotch peat, for instance? Is it the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The fuel was produced some years ago, and it was shown to be an admirable fuel, but it was a question of cost of production and handling. There is not the slightest doubt as to the quality of the peat and of the uses to which it may be put, if it is possible to put it on the market at a price that would enable it to compete with coal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have never been in Scotland, but my forefathers who came from there used to talk about peat. It was the fuel of many of the people in Scotland, and their way of drying it was very primitive and simple, and if we have the same sort of peat in Canada I do no| quite understand why the same results should not follow.

I presume the reason is because you have not the population in close proximity to the peat bog. May I ask the minister, in preparing his Estimates, what information is used in determining what work shall be done? Has the minister first hand knowledge of the needs of the various mining districts, or has his deputy? Has he visited the great asbestos mines in the Eastern Townships?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend must know that we are in touch with all parts of the country, and, as a matter of fact, we are covering the whole of Canada. My hon.

friend is speaking now largely of the work of the Geological Survey, which we are coming to. The greater part of our mines work is done, not over the country, but actually at the Mines Department, for instance, in our ore dressing laboratories and in other work. The main part of our work, so far as the country goes, is the work of the Geological Survey in mapping out various parts of the country, showing rock formations, what is likely to be developed, following up matters that arise, the deposits, their character and assays. The work is carried on from year to year, and to be valuable at all it has to he a continuous process. By the putting out of maps, which is the greater part of the work of the Geological Survey, the prospector is enabled to decide intelligently where he shall go with prospects of success.
Geological Survey, $270,400.

Perhaps the questions which I put before would come more properly in connection with this item. My information is that the expenditure of the department in regard to geological survey and other mining work is not by any means in proportion to the mineral production of the different parts of the country. For instance, Ontario produces a great deal of the, mineral wealth of the country, and the expenditure of the department is considerably beneath the proportion which one might expect to be spent in that province if the principle is that the expenditures should bear some relation to the mineral production. What is the principle of expenditure? Has the minister himself or his deputy visited several of the ' great mining districts of our country like the Sudbury nickel and copper mines, the asbestos mines in the Eastern Townships, the molybdenite mines near Sherbrooke; or the silver and gold districts in Porcupine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It would be pretty hard to lay down an exact ratio between the expenditure upon a matter like the geological survey and the results in the practical development of minek, because obviously you might discover, in one district in which you have been doing a little work, a highly mineralized area with posstbilities of development on an enormous scale. You might, on the other hand, do very considerable work in that district before any discoveries were made, and large expenditures would have to be made in order to get at the potentialities there. But in the long run I do not think I would be making an
exaggerated statement in saying that the development of our mining industry throughout Canada is very largely dependent upon the work of the Geological Survey. Let me give one or two illustrations of the kind of work we are endeavouring to do at present, and let me take the part of the country with which I am somewhat familiar, namely, the Cariboo gold mining district. When the gold rush to California was a thing of the past, all those men came up to the upper regions of the Fraser river where gold was discovered-my hon. friend knows a little of the history of that time. From that time up to within the last few years, something like $30,000,000 in gold was taken out of those various tributaries of the stream, sometimes by placer mining, sometimes by deep boring, pumping and so on. Many of those streams, the original beds which had gold in them, have been exhausted, and there have been immense problems to face in regard to reaching others on account of water and the costly method of pumping water, and the direction has also been lost. Last year we sent a man up there, and we have another man up there this year to try from the geological point of view to find out the old beds of these streams which have been diverted or overlaid by other material, and we have every reason to believe that we shall be able by Ithe work of the Geological Survey to determine the particular location of a great number of these old overgrown streams similar to those which have produced about $30,000,000 worth of gold, and when we have all that work done and the proper maps got out, I am not prophesying, because it is quite within the range of probability that nothing may turn up, but ton the other hand there may be an enormous gold production as the result of that work. It would be pretty difficult work, as regards gold, copper, asbestos or any other mineral to lay down an exact ratio between the expenditure and the result, because it must be guess work in any event. We are carrying on investigation work as regards such things as graphite, fluorite and other minerals. During the last two years we did a great deal of work as regards molybdenite and tungsten, which hitherto had hardly been known to occur in this country, but which, in the tremendous necessities of the war, led us to make various experiments; and We were able, by the Munitions Board buying, on behalf of the British Government, any molybdenite that was available, to stimulate the search for it, to discover a certain amount of it.

to have it milled and concentrated in our ore dressing laboratory here, and to do a great deal of stimulating -work of a very high character. That has been going on in connection with many minerals.
My own feeling about the Department of Mines is that perhaps we have not paid the attention to it in the past that we should have done. It is very hard to get the class of men required, and personally I think we should be very much more liberal in our expenditure on the Mines Department than we have been in the past.

We had the first Mines Department on the North American Continent, did we not?
iMr. BURRELL: Yes. I am confident that our Mines Department and 'Geological Survey contains as many first-class men in their line of work-most important and basic work -as does probably any other country in the world. Nearly every geologist of repute in Canada, if he is not in the Mines Departs ment, has been trained in the Geological Survey. We take men first as assistants in the field after they have had at least a two years' course at the university, and we do not admit them as geologists until they have taken their degree, and also a three years' post graduate course and have become a Doctor of Science or Ph. D. We have from sixteen to twenty such men in our service, not at very big salaries, and every now and then we are losing one or two. They are carrying on work the value of which lies in its continuity, and it is a serious matter when by reason of not having enough men, or not paying them enough, there is a break in the work, which has then to be left until we can get somebody else to take it up. We have lost a good many of our men in the war. Fortunately we are getting some of them back, but one or two unfortunately will never come back. If I were to continue as head of the department I should like to endeavour another year to enlarge the whole scope of the work, because I believe that it can be of immensely greater value to the country than perhaps we have realized.
Mr. McMA'STER: What is the future for the two minerals which are most abundant in the Eastern Townships, copper and asbestos?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend detailed information on that, not expecting my Estimates to come up this afternoon, but I shall be very glad

to take a note of it and let him have full information.
Has the minister ever visited the asbestos quarries there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have not. It is very difficult to visit all parts of Canada, and I am criticised for not visiting parts of my own province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is this geological research work carried on systematically? Is the whole province of Nova Scotia, for instance, covered?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: 'Speaking ibroadly, we are covering the whole country. In Nova Scotia we shall complete this year the geological mapping of areas at Lockeport and Sable River. It is also proposed to make the geological surveys necessary for the compilation of large scale plans of gold mines situate in Yarmouth county. Southwestern Nova Scotia will also be visited for the purpose of examining new developments and discoveries that have been made in that territory. The geological work necessary to a report on the Sydney coal area will also be completed this year. Further structural work will also be done in respect to the Malaguash salt deposits. My hon. friend will understand that it may take geologists three years to get sufficient data before they can put out a map which will be of real value to the man who is going in to take up development work; it is necessarily continuous work. During the war we have practically confined our attention to work that would give immediate results. Answering my hon. friend's question broadly, I would say yes, we cover the whole country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the department reports on the researches of Mr. Fletcher, for instance? He is a very able man and has been in the department many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We have a complete record of every geologist's work, and I will make a point of looking up the reports my hon. friend refers to and let him have copies.
Grant to the Canadian Mining Institute, $3,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there any co-operation in research work and the testing of minerals, and so forth, between the Dominion and the provincial departments of mines? In Nova Scotia, for instance, we have a pretty well organized department of mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: All our officers keep in touch with the work of the provincial departments. Only recently we had a communication from the Minister of Mines in Nova Scotia with reference to assistance in regard to the salt deposits I spoke of just now, and which they thought were possibly of commercial value. We are only too glad to co-operate in every way we can and to put at the disposal of the provinces any of our experts who can help them in the solution of any problem that will enure to their benefit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We get very excellent results from co-operation between the Dominion and provincial governments in the matter of agriculture, for instance, and I see no reason why we should not get good results from co-operation between the departments of mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Our department keeps in sympathetic touch with the provincial departments and we are always ready to cooperate.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: While we are obliged to ask for this vote to cover the expenses of the Canada Trade Commission, it is not expected that it will cost the country anything as a charge is made for all Canadian goods that are sold under credit. We expect that there will be no cost to the country for the administration of the Commission.
What trade commissioners have we, apart from special commissioners, operating in Canada or in other parts of the world?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
We passed the
item which relates to my honourable friend's question and I am perhaps hardly in a position to answer him accurately. We have in Australia a trade commissioner, Mr. D. H. Ross, who is at present in Canada. We have a commissioner in China; his name also is Ross and he is at present in Canada. We have two commissioners in South America, one in Scotland and one in England.
Have you one in Holland?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: We have none in Holland.

You have an agent in
Rotterdam?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I do not think we have a trade agent in Rotterdam.
You have a representative; I have been in his office many times.
What is his name?
I forget at this moment.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend is correct. 'It is proposed to extend the number of our trade commissioners abroad, but just at the present time, owing to the difficulties in carrying on trade, it has not been deemed advisable to increase the number. When normal trade conditions are resumed the world over, I think we may very profitably appoint further commissioners.

The reason I mention this particular branch of the service is that from information which has come to me-and I do not wish to specify-there are certain of the trade commissioners of Canada who are absolutely out of date, unqualified to



perform the reasonable functions of trade commissioners and have been " asleep at the switch for many years, as I think they will admit themselves. They have not been in complete touch with the Government and are not energetically carrying on the work for which they were appointed. ' I would like the minister to take notice of the conditions and see if the whole system should not be surveyed and. possibly bettered by replacing these men and putting younger and more aggressive men in the service.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's criticism is hardly applicable to recent appointments. The present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has made it a practice in recent years to appoint young men with university education and some little business experience and capacity. I think that my hon. friend's remarks might possibly be true in reference to some of the older appointments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can the minister point to any results which have come to us by reason of these trade agents or commissioners, or are they merely figureheads, or gentlemen abroad disporting themselves at the expense of the country? Unless the trade of this country is expanding by reason of these gentlemen being, here and there as representing us; unless we are getting advantages in trade; unless our trade is increasing and new avenues are being opened up to Canada by reason of these commissioners, they would not appear to me to be serving any useful purpose. I presume that these agents are supposed to make a report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce every year, and it would be interesting to know how the trade of Canada is developing in the places where they are operating. It would be well for them to understand that the Parliament of Canada has a keen eye upon this service in different parts of tlm world and that we are anxious to see what they are doing. If they are, as the hon. member for North Perth '(Mr. Morphy) said, " asleep at the switch," we might as well take them home, leave the switch alone, or appoint somebody else who will earn the salary and work to the greater advantage of the country. I am not speaking with anybody in view, but I have reason to suspect that in many instances we are not getting any great practical results from this service.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
It is very difficult for me to answer in detail my hon. friend's criticism, but I think it cannot be said of any of our commissioners that they do not

earn their salaries or do not perform a service to Canada. I know that in the case of the South African agent, Mr. Egan, trade has been developed owing to his efforts and the department is very much impressed with his work. The same might be said of Mr. Ross in Australia. I think in every case they have performed a valuable service.

That is also my impression. Last year I was for a number of weeks in Holland, particularly in Rotterdam. I had the opportunity of going through the office of the representative of the Canadian Trade and Commerce Department in that city, and though it was during the war I could judge what an amount of work that official was performing and what important service he was rendering to Canadian trade in the way of imparting valuable information. Although at that time transportation facilities were curtailed to a large degree, he was able to supply any amount of useful information which will be available now that the war is ended. In the city of Antwerp there was formerly a Canadian trade agent but a few weeks,, or a few days perhaps, before the war broke out, he died, and the vacancy caused by his death has not yet been filled. Antwerp, while not the city it was in the past, is an important port of embarkation for passengers, including emigrants, and I look upon the trade agency there as invaluable and almost indispensable in the interests of Canada. I would urge upon the minister to replace the trade agent there immediately. No doubt at an early date Belgians will be seeking admission to this country, especially gardeners, who will be most useful to Canada, because our population does not consume sufficient vegetables, a fact which is well known to the medical profession. We need very badly the presence in Canada of Belgian gardeners, and we should invite those men to come here, but they will not embark upon the enterprise unless they can be supplied with proper information regarding this country. A Canadian trade agent in Antwerp would meet that requirement adequately. I imagine the vacancy in the office of trade agent is to be filled, and I would urge the minister to take the question up immediately. I have nobody particular in my mind, but if the minister wants me to select a trade agent for him I can assure him I will recommend the best man that is available either here or in Belgium.

speechtext:

$350,000 is asked for in the event of some city corps being called out to drill at their own local headquarters. speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I do not speak definitely, but my recollection is that every person under the Act as it now stands must pass an examination. Under the amendments proposed in the Bill, which is likely to stand over until next session, it was intended to abandon the general Civil Service examination, and applicants for appointment to the Service would be required to pass an examination having reference to the position to be filled. It seems to me that candidates for the Civil Service who possess the degree of bachelor of arts from any of our universities ought not to be required to pass the ordinary examination. speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: I have no doubt that under the classification, a university degree might be accepted so far as the general educational qualifications were concerned. But in all cases where special duties are to be performed the applicant would have to pass an examination thereon.

I asked the question because I think that the system which has been followed, and which I understand from the minister is intended to be followed,

strikes me as absolutely ridiculous. The examinations set by the Civil Service Commission are in many oases no test at all, -catchy questions which are not a test of a man's qualifications. You have only to look over the examination papers of the past to agree with me in that, Mr. Chairman. Why should not a university degree be accepted for at least the great bulk of the positions in the Civil Service? In fact, I think the standard of matriculation as indicative of a oandidaJte's general education might very well be accepted for nine-tenths of the positions in the service. I did not understand that.

Might I draw the attention of my hon. friend to the salaries of the commissioners? How is it that the commissioners, appointed with the understanding that they would have the status of deputy ministers, do not receive the salaries of deputy ministers? They receive $5,000, while deputy ministers receive $6,000. I remember that some years ago, when this commission was created the right hon. the Prime Minister, who ithen led the Opposition stated that in his judgment the commissioners should be considered as judges as to their tenure of office.
They were given responsibilities which would certainly entitle them to the status of deputy ministers. In my judgment, their responsibilities are as great as, if not greater than, those of ordinary deputy ministers, and I do not see why Mr. Eoehe, Mr. Jameson and Mr. La Eochelle should not be treated as deputy ministers. In paragraph 2, section 9, of the Act creating the Civil Service Commission, I find the following:
The rank, standing and salary of each commissioner shall be that of Deputy Minister of a department and each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
The Act of 1912, providing for the addition of one member to the commission confirmed the status of the commissioners in the following words:
The rank, standing and salary of each commissioner shall be those of a deputy head of a

department and each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour and shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
The Civil Service Act of 1918 also confirms the status of the commissioners in the following terms:
The rank and standing of each commissioner shall be that of a deputy head. Each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and the House of Commons.
I hold no brief for the commission, but as their rank and status have been repeatedly fixed by Act of Parliament, and as we have increased the salaries of deputy ministers from 55,000 to $6,000, I .do not see why the Civil Service Commissioners, having regard to the responsibilities of the office, should not be treated on a footing of equality with deputy ministers.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Personally I am not disposed to disagree with what my hon. friend says. For certain purposes-, therefore, officials are sometimes given the rank of deputy head.
Am I to understand that by the legislation which will be brought down next session, these commissioners will be placed on the basis that I have suggested?
